title: SPONSORED: How to Evaluate CPU Performance for Agentic AI
gist: In this Arm-sponsored piece, Arm argues that agentic AI makes the CPU central again: the CPU market is forecast to grow from $26B in 2025 to $246B five years later. Arm proposes measuring CPUs at the core, system and rack level, with tasks per rack and energy per task as the metrics that count. Arm claims a third-party evaluation shows its AGI CPU delivering about 2X the performance per rack of AMD EPYC 9755.

insights.claim: The CPU market is expected to grow from $26 billion in 2025 to $246 billion five years later, with most of that growth coming from AI host CPUs and agentic AI sandboxes.
insights.speaker: Timothy Pricket-Morgan
insights.so_what: This implies a roughly 9.5x expansion (about 57% CAGR) in the CPU TAM, a bullish signal for Arm, AMD and Intel server CPUs, though the forecast's source is not cited.
insights.quote: the CPU market is expected to grow from $26 billion in 2025 to $246 billion only five years later
insights.locator: A funny thing happened on the way

insights.claim: The article argues that agentic AI has made the CPU central again after GPUs and XPUs temporarily displaced it, because sequential latency on the agent loop's critical path is the CPU's strength.
insights.speaker: Timothy Pricket-Morgan
insights.so_what: As agentic workloads grow, share of AI compute spending shifts back toward CPUs.
insights.quote: sequential latency – the bailiwick of the CPU
insights.locator: When it comes to agentic AI

insights.claim: In systems where accelerator inference is part of the agent loop, CPU delays in scheduling, orchestration and data preparation stretch the task path and leave GPUs underused, so faster CPUs return work to accelerators sooner.
insights.speaker: Jeff Defilippi
insights.so_what: CPU quality becomes a lever on GPU return on investment, which supports pricier host CPUs in AI servers.
insights.quote: Reducing latency in the CPU-visible portions of that path can move the agent to its next action sooner and, where accelerators are involved, return work to the GPU or XPU sooner as well.

insights.claim: Arm's Defilippi argues that agentic workflows have both a latency problem and a concurrency problem: dependent steps accumulate latency along the critical path, while many concurrent agents demand core count, memory bandwidth, cache capacity and scheduling efficiency.
insights.speaker: Jeff Defilippi
insights.so_what: CPU designs that pair strong single-thread performance with high core counts and memory bandwidth win, which favors high-core-count server parts.
insights.quote: Many agentic workflows therefore have both a latency problem and a concurrency problem

insights.claim: Where inference serving is in the agent loop, CPU-visible functions such as scheduling, tokenization, serialization and KV-cache management put pressure on memory, which makes memory bandwidth per core and memory locality key.
insights.speaker: Jeff Defilippi
insights.so_what: This is a second-order tailwind for server memory bandwidth (DRAM content per socket).

insights.claim: Arm argues that because a single agentic task dynamically chains model calls, retrieval, database transactions, code execution and tool calls, successful task completion is a more meaningful unit of performance than any single component metric.
insights.speaker: Jeff Defilippi
insights.so_what: If buyers adopt task-level metrics, the benchmarks that set procurement could shift away from SPEC-style per-core scores.
insights.quote: That makes successful task completion, not any single component metric, the more meaningful unit of performance.
insights.locator: Multi-tier and stateful computing are not new

insights.claim: Arm says it is not pushing a single golden agentic AI benchmark but a methodology that combines component benchmarks such as InferenceX and TPCx-AI with agentic workload measurements and end-to-end task evaluation.
insights.speaker: Timothy Pricket-Morgan
insights.so_what: Existing benchmarks miss CPU-side orchestration, sandboxing and state management, which leaves room for vendors to define new metrics.
insights.quote: Arm is not advocating for some kind of golden agentic AI benchmark.
insights.locator: By the way, Arm is not advocating

insights.claim: Arm proposes evaluating CPUs at three levels: per-thread latency for critical-path work at the core level; throughput, concurrency, memory behavior and sustained performance under high utilization at the system level; and completed work within power, cooling and physical constraints at the rack level.
insights.speaker: Timothy Pricket-Morgan
insights.so_what: This gives buyers a reusable evaluation rubric, and Arm's framing tilts toward density and efficiency, where it competes best.
insights.locator: That leads to a practical way

insights.claim: Infrastructure teams are urged to test CPUs under realistic load and concurrency, not lightly loaded peak results, because sustained performance under high utilization drives agent throughput.
insights.speaker: Timothy Pricket-Morgan
insights.so_what: Headline peak benchmarks may mislead buyers sizing agentic fleets.
insights.quote: Infrastructure teams should therefore evaluate performance under realistic load and concurrency rather than relying only on lightly loaded peak results.

insights.claim: Arm argues that because datacenters run within fixed power, cooling and physical limits, tasks per rack and energy per task become the decisive metrics, with row-level economics possibly next.
insights.speaker: Jeff Defilippi
insights.so_what: Power-constrained buyers will favor efficient CPUs, which is a structural argument for Arm-based servers.
insights.quote: That is why metrics such as tasks per rack and energy per task become important alongside CPU-level performance

insights.claim: Arm says a third party it sanctioned evaluated its AGI CPU against AMD EPYC Turin on agentic tooling, orchestration and reasoning/planning workloads, and that rack-level modeling built on measured server-level results showed about 2X the performance per rack of AMD EPYC 9755.
insights.speaker: Timothy Pricket-Morgan
insights.so_what: This is a vendor-sponsored claim built on modeling rather than measured racks, but it signals Arm going after AMD's x86 server share in AI hosts.
insights.quote: the results show approximately 2X the performance per rack compared with AMD EPYC 9755
insights.locator: The testing uses measured server-level performance

insights.claim: The article notes that latency-versus-concurrency trade-offs will persist over the next four to five years, which matches the service life of machines being installed today, even though agentic workloads are hard to predict.
insights.speaker: Timothy Pricket-Morgan
insights.so_what: Today's CPU purchases lock in agentic capacity through about 2030, which raises the stakes on choosing an architecture.
insights.locator: As has always been the case

insights.claim: Hyperscalers, neoclouds, sovereign AI centers and enterprises will have to balance limiting CPU SKUs in their fleets against matching hardware to distinct parts of agentic workflows, which the article calls possibly the most complex capacity planning job IT has faced.
insights.speaker: Timothy Pricket-Morgan
insights.so_what: More SKU specialization and heavier reliance on vendor advisory could favor vendors with broad portfolios and system makers.
insights.quote: this may be the most complex capacity planning job that IT organizations have ever encountered
insights.locator: When all is said and done
